Whatever ’tis, whose beauty here below Attracts thee thus and makes thee stream and flow, And wind and curl, and wink and smile, Shifting thy gate and guile; Though thy close commerce nought at all imbars My present search, for eagles eye not stars, And still the lesser by the best And highest good is blest; Yet, seeing all things that subsist and be, Have their commissions from divinity, And teach us duty, I will see What man may learn from thee. First, I am sure, the subject so respected Is well dispos’d, for bodies once infected, Deprav’d, or dead, can have with thee No hold, nor sympathy. Next, there’s in it a restless, pure desire And longing for thy bright and vital fire, Desire that never will be quench’d, Nor can be writh’d, nor wrench’d. These are the magnets which so strongly move And work all night upon thy light and love, As beauteous shapes, we know not why, Command and guide the eye. For where desire, celestial, pure desire Hath taken root, and grows, and doth not tire, There God a commerce states, and sheds His secret on their heads. This is the heart he craves, and who so will But give it him, and grudge not, he shall feel That God is true, as herbs unseen Put on their youth and green.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Whatever, Attracts, And

outputs.L1:
Whatever ’tis whose beauty here below  
Attracts thee thus, and makes thee stream and flow,  
And wind and curl, and wink and smile,  
Shifting thy gait and guile;  

Though thy close commerce nought at all debars  
My present search—for eagles eye not stars,  
And still the lesser by the best  
And highest good is blessed—  

Yet, seeing all things that subsist and be  
Have their commissions from divinity,  
And teach us duty, I will see  
What man may learn from thee.  

First, I am sure the subject so respected  
Is well disposed; for bodies once infected,  
Depraved, or dead, can have with thee  
No hold nor sympathy.  

Next, there is in it a restless, pure desire,  
A longing for thy bright and vital fire—  
Desire that never will be quenched,  
Nor can be writhed nor wrenched.  

These are the magnets that so strongly move  
And work all night upon thy light and love,  
As beauteous shapes, we know not why,  
Command and guide the eye.  

For where desire—celestial, pure desire—  
Hath taken root, and grows, and doth not tire,  
There God a commerce states, and sheds  
His secret on their heads.  

This is the heart He craves; and whoso will  
But give it Him, and grudge not, he shall feel  
That God is true, as herbs unseen  
Put on their youth and green.
outputs.L2:
Whatever earthly loveliness draws you so powerfully that you pour onward, twist and coil, flash and gleam, continually changing your movement and your subtle ways, your hidden intimacy with it does not prevent my present inquiry. Eagles do not fix their sight upon the stars, and lesser things are always enriched by what is best and highest. Yet because everything that exists receives its purpose from God and teaches us our obligations, I will consider what lesson humanity may take from you.

First, I am certain that the object of such attention must be rightly ordered, since anything diseased, corrupted, or lifeless can neither connect nor sympathize with you. Second, it possesses a pure and unceasing hunger for your radiant, life-giving flame—a longing that cannot be extinguished, distorted, or torn away.

These qualities act like magnets, powerfully drawing upon your brightness and affection throughout the night, just as beautiful forms direct the gaze for reasons we cannot explain. Wherever a holy and untainted desire has taken root, continues to grow, and never weakens, God establishes communion there and pours his hidden wisdom upon those who possess it.

This is the kind of heart God seeks. Whoever freely gives such a heart to him, without reluctance, will discover that God is faithful, just as plants hidden from sight renew themselves and become young and green again.
outputs.L3:
The speaker turns to a beautiful, flowing phenomenon in nature and asks it for spiritual instruction, recognizing that both its existence and its purpose come from God. Its grace and movement reveal something of the divine order, yet only a soul that is pure, receptive, and rightly disposed can truly sympathize with such beauty and answer its silent call.

Within that soul burns a restless and unquenchable longing for heavenly light. This yearning draws it beyond earthly appearances and toward the love of God. Pure celestial desire works like a magnet upon the heart, directing it toward its divine source just as visible beauty naturally attracts and guides the eye.

Those who freely surrender their hearts to God will come to know His truth not merely as an idea, but as a living and renewing power. His grace restores what seems hidden, dormant, or lifeless, just as unseen herbs spring up and become green again when touched by life-giving water and light.
outputs.L4:
The speaker pauses before a mysterious form of earthly beauty, wondering what hidden power causes it to turn so faithfully toward the light. Its movement seems more than a natural instinct: it reflects a deeper spiritual order woven into creation. Nature responds to the light without hesitation, and in doing so offers humanity a lesson. Just as living things seek the source of their growth, the human soul is meant to turn toward God, the source of truth, goodness, and life.

This pattern reveals that creation is not separate from divine meaning. The natural world quietly demonstrates how desire can guide a being toward fulfillment. A sincere longing for God is itself the beginning of spiritual transformation, because divine grace answers the heart that remains receptive and steadfast. When that desire is pure and persistent, even a soul that seems barren or hidden can be renewed.

The speaker therefore ends in confidence rather than uncertainty. God’s truth is not reserved only for those who possess special knowledge or outward advantages. It can enter any heart that opens itself to divine light. Just as plants concealed from ordinary sight may nevertheless take root, grow, and become green, the inward life of faith can flourish through grace. Nature’s hidden growth thus becomes a sign of spiritual hope: whoever continually turns toward God may receive illumination, renewal, and life.
outputs.L5:
### Whatever Attracts and Inspires

Whatever attracts our attention often reveals something about who we are. A beautiful landscape may awaken a desire for peace, while an ambitious idea may inspire creativity and change. We are naturally drawn to people, places, and experiences that reflect our hopes or satisfy our curiosity.

Yet attraction is only the beginning. What truly matters is how we respond and what we choose to pursue. By paying attention to whatever attracts us—and understanding why—we can discover new interests, form meaningful connections, and move toward a more fulfilling life.

**The Star**

Whatever ’tis, whose beauty here below  
Attracts thee thus and makes thee stream and flow,  
And wind and curl, and wink and smile,  
Shifting thy gate and guile;

Though thy close commerce nought at all imbars  
My present search, for eagles eye not stars,  
And still the lesser by the best  
And highest good is blest;

Yet, seeing all things that subsist and be  
Have their commissions from divinity,  
And teach us duty, I will see  
What man may learn from thee.

First, I am sure, the subject so respected  
Is well disposed, for bodies once infected,  
Deprav’d, or dead, can have with thee  
No hold, nor sympathy.

Next, there’s in it a restless, pure desire  
And longing for thy bright and vital fire,  
Desire that never will be quench’d,  
Nor can be writh’d, nor wrench’d.

These are the magnets which so strongly move  
And work all night upon thy light and love,  
As beauteous shapes, we know not why,  
Command and guide the eye.

For where desire, celestial, pure desire  
Hath taken root, and grows, and doth not tire,  
There God a commerce states, and sheds  
His secret on their heads.

This is the heart he craves, and who so will  
But give it him, and grudge not, he shall feel  
That God is true, as herbs unseen  
Put on their youth and green.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide the text of the seventeenth-century devotional poem that begins, “Whatever ’tis, whose beauty here below / Attracts thee thus and makes thee stream and flow.”
counterfactuals.output:
### Divine Love  
*John Norris of Bemerton (1657–1712)*

Whatever ’tis, whose beauty here below  
Attracts thee thus and makes thee stream and flow,  
The same in greater measure thou shalt see  
In God, from all defect and mixture free.  
Then let not dust thy soul’s affection move:  
Who sees the Godhead sure must die for love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2
